back: Better-adapted individuals survive and reproduce more, passing on their alleles, so the frequency of those alleles increases over generations.
An environmental factor (predator, disease, climate, chemical) that affects survival and reproduction of different phenotypes.
Extremes selected against: mean unchanged, range narrower (e.g. human birth mass).
One extreme favoured, often after environmental change: the mean shifts (e.g. antibiotic resistance).
Both extremes favoured, intermediates selected against: two peaks may form.
Vertical: parent to offspring by binary fission. Horizontal: between bacteria, e.g. plasmids by conjugation.

front: Why is Hb^S common where malaria is common?
back: Heterozygotes are partly protected against severe malaria (heterozygote advantage), so the allele is maintained.

front: Does an antibiotic cause resistance mutations?
back: No. Mutations are random; the antibiotic selects bacteria that already carry resistance alleles.
